vocabulary.zh:
n. 经济学者, 经济家
[经] 经济学家
vocabulary.en: n. an expert in the science of economics
vocabulary.example: It’s not a question about whether fireworks celebrations are enjoyable, but whether the people enjoying them are aware of – or actually paying for – their full cost. Economists call this a “negative externality”. A purchase benefits the buyer and seller, but some of its costs fall on people outside that transaction. Fireworks offer a particularly visible example because the enjoyment is concentrated in time while the consequences are spread among households, public services and wildlife. As a finance researcher, I think this concept is overlooked in the fireworks debate.

The UK’s official air-quality monitoring has recorded short-lived spikes in fine particles around Bonfire Night, although bonfires also contribute and weather affects how quickly smoke disperses. cloze.title: 四选一完形填空
cloze.instruction: 阅读节选，为每一空选择最符合原文语境的选项，每题只有一个正确答案。

parts.text: It’s not a question about whether fireworks celebrations are enjoyable, but whether the people enjoying them are

of – or actually paying for – their full cost. Economists call this a “negative externality”. A purchase benefits the buyer and seller, but some of its costs fall on people outside that transaction. Fireworks offer a particularly visible example because the

is concentrated in time while the consequences are spread among households, public services and wildlife. As a finance researcher, I think this concept is overlooked in the fireworks debate.

Consider injuries. Figures show that 123 hospital

in England attributed to fireworks in 2024–25. That is not a count of everyone injured: cases treated without hospital admission are excluded. Preventing such injuries may not cut the NHS budget, but it can free

time for other patients. In an overstretched health service, that is an economic benefit even if it never appears as a saving in the Treasury’s accounts.

Pollution creates another unpriced cost. The UK’s official air-quality monitoring has recorded

spikes in fine particles around Bonfire Night, although bonfires also contribute and weather affects how quickly smoke disperses. The Department for Environment, Food and Rural Affairs assigns a central estimated

cost of £114,411 per tonne of fine particulate emissions (known as PM2.5), expressed in 2025 prices to account for inflation. This is not a figure for fireworks: calculating that would require information about their emissions and who is

. It does show why a product can have an environmental cost that never appears on its receipt.

Nature belongs on the balance sheet

The damage is not limited to human health. In a peer-reviewed Dutch study, researchers found that
1,000 times as many birds were flying during New Year’s Eve fireworks as on ordinary nights. The disruption extended several miles from the displays. The exact scale cannot be

to British Bonfire Nights, but the finding challenges the idea that fireworks affect only those who choose to watch.

Birds forced into sudden flight expend energy and lose opportunities to rest. Pets and livestock may also be distressed. Alongside noise and smoke, spent casings and other waste leave a physical
. Sustainability means considering these effects, not simply asking how much carbon a celebration emits.

reading.title: 主旨、理解与信息定位
reading.instruction: 阅读原文后回答 5 道选择题：1 道主旨、1 道内容理解、1 道段落细节、2 道信息定位。段落细节题以题干指定段落为准。

questions.prompt: Which statement best summarises the overall focus of this article?
options: Victorian spiritualism turned the desire to communicate beyond death into commercial opportunities.
Consumers' ideas about organic food do not always match what labels and standards communicate.
Climate-related risks discourage investment in poorer countries and can also harm corporations.
Fireworks create environmental and economic costs that outlast the celebrations.
questions.explanation: 把标题与全文各段的中心内容连起来判断主旨，避免把同一主题下的其他话题当成本文重点。
questions.evidence: It’s not a question about whether fireworks celebrations are enjoyable, but whether the people enjoying them are aware of – or actually paying for – their full cost.

questions.prompt: What economic issue is central to the fireworks discussion?
options: Whether every celebration should last the same number of minutes
Whether the seller's displayed price captures every social cost automatically
Whether users bear the full costs imposed by their enjoyment
Whether fireworks are colourful enough to photograph
questions.explanation: 第 2 段提供了作答依据。正确选项用不同说法表达了文中的信息；请比较范围、数量、因果关系与限定词。
questions.evidence: It’s not a question about whether fireworks celebrations are enjoyable, but whether the people enjoying them are aware of – or actually paying for – their full cost.

questions.prompt: Which of the following statements is explicitly made in paragraph 6?

Policymakers now have an opportunity to assess the social costs alongside safety, business impacts and cultural value.
A purchase benefits the buyer and seller, but some of its costs fall on people outside that transaction.
In a peer-reviewed Dutch study, researchers found that approximately 1,000 times as many birds were flying during New Year’s Eve fireworks as on ordinary nights.
questions.explanation: 定位第 6 段，比较四个选项的具体信息。其余选项来自本文其他段落，并非本段明确陈述的内容。
questions.evidence: In a peer-reviewed Dutch study, researchers found that approximately 1,000 times as many birds were flying during New Year’s Eve fireworks as on ordinary nights.
